Gastroenterology · published research

Colitis

Animal colitis studies often report lower disease scores and inflammation after PBM, with effects varying by sex, dose, wavelength, and delivery route. Human treatment evidence remains limited to one uncontrolled report.

PBM Database summary

What the records report

Animal colitis studies often report lower disease scores and inflammation after PBM, with effects varying by sex, dose, wavelength, and delivery route. Human treatment evidence remains limited to one uncontrolled report.

Summary of the Evidence

The exact “Colitis” category contains eight animal publications, mostly mouse or rat experiments using chemically induced disease. They include red or near-infrared PBM and broader visible-light phototherapy, which should not all be treated as the same intervention. Related categories add one 81-patient uncontrolled ulcerative-colitis report, an inflammatory-bowel-disease feasibility protocol without results, an animal study of lung effects secondary to bowel inflammation, and a stem-cell combination study. The two 2023 rat papers share investigators but use different local and vascular delivery questions; the database does not establish whether their animals overlapped.

Human and clinical evidence

The 1999 single-arm report described reduced pain and stool frequency in 72% of 81 people after transanal He-Ne laser sessions and reported mucosal improvement on colonoscopy. Without a control group, these observations cannot separate treatment from natural fluctuation or concurrent care; the English full text was not located. A later feasibility protocol addresses fatigue, depression, and pain in people with IBD, but it provides no efficacy results. Thus, direct clinical evidence for controlling colitis remains very limited.

Animal evidence

Across chemically induced rat and mouse models, PBM studies commonly report lower disease-activity scores, less inflammatory-cell infiltration, reduced myeloperoxidase or cytokine measures, improved mucus or barrier measures, and less histologic injury. A 2023 sex-comparison study using 660-nm red LED found reductions in disease score, mast-cell degranulation, and several inflammatory markers in both sexes; some histology and cytokine changes appeared only in males. A companion experiment found that local abdominal PBM improved intestinal histology, whereas transcutaneous tail-vein treatment did not, although both altered mucus and inflammatory measures (Bitencourt et al. 2023; Rodrigues et al. 2023).

Other reports include 830-nm near-infrared treatment with improved disease scores, colon length, and histology in mice, and red or 940-nm LED studies reporting less edema, ulceration, or inflammatory activity. A blue-versus-red-versus-green comparison found wavelength- and intensity-dependent results. A separate full-spectrum lamp experiment is broad visible-light phototherapy, not a direct test of narrow-band PBM. A stem-cell study also found benefit after cells were preconditioned with PBM; that combination does not isolate direct bowel irradiation. The overall preclinical direction is often favorable, but not every route, dose, or outcome performs alike (Maeng et al. 2026; Zigmond et al. 2014).

In-vitro and ex-vivo evidence

No standalone cell-culture study directly tests PBM treatment of colitis. One related mixed study preconditioned adipose-derived stem cells with PBM before transferring them into mice; this is indirect combination evidence, not direct treatment of the bowel with light.

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

Protocols range from 660-nm red visible LEDs and 940-nm near-infrared LEDs to 830-nm abdominal irradiation, blue or green visible light, and broad-spectrum lamps. Studies differ in fluence, intensity, treatment frequency, sex, disease model, shaved versus unshaved skin, and local versus vascular delivery. The 2023 rat protocol used 660-nm light at 100 mW for 150 seconds across three points; other studies used different schedules. There is no agreed dose or clinical route.

Interpretation

The animal evidence supports further testing because several models show lower inflammation and tissue injury, while also demonstrating that response depends on protocol and model. The single uncontrolled human report is not enough to show that PBM controls colitis in patients. A well-controlled clinical trial with validated symptoms, endoscopy, medication use, and safety outcomes is still needed.

Evidence strength in source summaryLow for short-term disease and tissue outcomes across animal colitis models Very low for control of colitis in people
Publications and records12 relevant articles

Evidence strength rationale and next steps

Several mouse and rat experiments report lower disease scores, less tissue injury, and reduced inflammatory measures, although the models and light protocols differ. Human support is limited to one old uncontrolled report, and a feasibility protocol has no results. Independent replication and controlled patient trials using symptoms and endoscopic outcomes would be needed to judge clinical benefit.
